Milwaukee vs DEWALT Impact Wrench: Which 1/2-Inch Impact?

The short answer: the Milwaukee M18 1/2-inch makes 1,400 ft-lb of breakaway torque for $277.89. The DEWALT DCF899B makes 1,200 ft-lb for $239.99. On paper that is 200 ft-lb for $38. In practice, the anvil design and the batteries you already own decide this, not the torque number.

Why the Anvil Choice Matters More Than 200 ft-lb

A friction ring holds a socket by gripping the anvil with a steel ring. A socket slides on and off with a firm pull, and it stays put. A hog ring uses a pinched wire ring that bites harder into the socket's detent. It holds more securely and takes more effort to remove.

Practically: if you are swapping between a 17mm and a 21mm socket all afternoon, friction ring is the one you want. If you are hanging off a rusty suspension bolt and a dropped socket costs you 20 minutes, hog ring will not let go.

This is the kind of thing that reads as a footnote in a spec sheet and is the actual difference you feel every single day. I would take the anvil I want over the extra 200 ft-lb.

Does 200 ft-lb Matter?

For lug nuts, no. A passenger car lug nut spec is typically 80 to 100 ft-lb, and a half-ton truck is around 150. Both of these wrenches exceed that by an order of magnitude, and both will walk a wheel off without breathing hard.

Where breakaway torque earns its keep is rust. A crank pulley bolt that has been soaking in road salt for twelve winters does not care what the torque spec says. Breakaway rating is also measured as a peak number, not sustained output, so the real-world gap between 1,200 and 1,400 ft-lb is smaller than it looks.

The honest read: buy the extra torque if you live somewhere with road salt and work on old vehicles. Buy the cheaper one if you work on cars five years old or newer.

The Batteries You Already Own

This decides more purchases than torque ever does, and it should. Both of these are bare tools that need a platform. If you already have M18 batteries on a drill and an impact driver, the Milwaukee is the only sensible answer, and the same is true in reverse for 20V MAX.

Buying into the wrong platform costs more than either wrench. Price a charger and two batteries before you compare the tool prices, because that math usually flips the answer.

One honest thing: neither of these is a first impact wrench. They will shear a bolt head off before you realize you were at full trigger. If you are starting out, an impact wrench comparison with a lower-torque or pneumatic option is a better place to start, and the impact wrench review covers what happened when I used the big one on something it was too strong for.

Verdict

Buy the Milwaukee M18 if you are already on M18 batteries, or you want the most breakaway torque and a friction ring that swaps sockets fast.

Buy the DEWALT DCF899B if you are on 20V MAX, want the three-speed control for delicate fasteners, or just want to spend $38 less on almost the same tool.

Either way, pair it with impact-rated sockets. A chrome hand socket on one of these shatters, and that is a separate $30 problem you do not want to discover at 100 ft-lb. The impact socket set review covers why, and a torque wrench finishes the job that the impact starts.
